lead: Two systems can do the same job with chips from different families. The processor is chosen by the pattern of arithmetic the workload repeats, by how much memory it needs, by the power budget and by how many boards you will build. A microprocessor is a CPU alone and needs chips around it. A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one die. A DSP is shaped for multiply-accumulate. An SoC puts a complete system, radio included, on one die. This chapter shows which one fits which workload.
prereq: You need the hardware blocks from chapter 1.4 and the cost, power and time-to-market metrics from chapter 1.3.

blocks.text: A microprocessor is a CPU on its own chip. Its address bus, data bus and control lines come out on pins, so RAM, ROM, timers and I/O ports must be separate chips wired to it. The 8086 is the classic teaching example; an ARM Cortex-A in a phone is the modern one. The board is bigger and costs more, but you are free to attach any amount of DRAM, any flash and any peripheral chip.

A microcontroller (MCU) puts the CPU, flash program memory, SRAM, timers, serial ports, an ADC and GPIO on one die. A complete system then needs no extra chips beyond a crystal and a few passives. The 8051, PIC16 and ARM Cortex-M are the standard families.

Why the MCU exists: fewer chips means a smaller board, lower cost, lower power, fewer solder joints to fail, and predictable timing because program and data memory sit on-chip. The price is fixed supply. You get the flash and RAM the part was built with, and the peripherals it was built with, and nothing more.

items: Pick a microprocessor when the job needs an operating system, megabytes of DRAM, a display, or heavy general computing.
Pick a microcontroller when the job is sensors, keys, motors and control loops at kilohertz to low megahertz rates.
Memory sizing for either choice is covered in chapter 1.7.

sections.h3: DSP: a processor shaped for multiply-accumulate

blocks.text: Audio, video, motor control, radar and biomedical signals all run the same sum: y[n] = Σ h[k] · x[n − k], for k = 0 to N − 1. Each output sample needs N MAC operations. A MAC is one multiply plus one add; it counts as one MAC but two arithmetic operations.
A general CPU spends several cycles and several instructions per MAC. A DSP is built to do one MAC per cycle, using these blocks:

items: A hardware MAC unit that computes a × b + c in a single cycle.
Separate program and data buses (Harvard organisation, see chapter 1.6) so an instruction and its two operands arrive in the same cycle.
A barrel shifter that scales a value by any number of bits in one cycle.
Saturating arithmetic: an overflow clips to the largest value instead of wrapping round. A wrapped audio sample is heard as a loud click.
Address generators that update circular-buffer pointers with no extra instruction, plus zero-overhead loops for the filter inner loop.

blocks.text: A digital signal controller (DSC) is an MCU with DSP features added: a MAC unit and DSP addressing modes on a flash microcontroller that also has ADC and PWM. Motor control drives use them, because the same chip runs the control loop and the fast current loop.

sections.h3: SoC, ASIC and FPGA: the whole system on one die

blocks.text: A SoC (system on chip) holds a complete system on one die: one or more CPU cores, a GPU, a DRAM controller, a radio for Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, an audio codec, USB, and camera interfaces. A phone processor is the standard case. Short on-chip wires give high speed at low energy per operation, but nothing can be changed after the chip is manufactured.

Two production routes exist for a custom SoC. An ASIC fixes the design in silicon: the mask set costs a large one-time payment called NRE (non-recurring engineering), but the cost per chip is very low once volume is high. An FPGA is logic configured after manufacture: no mask cost, so NRE is essentially zero and time-to-market is short, but each board costs more and burns more power. High volume and low power point to ASIC; small volume and changing requirements point to FPGA or a ready-made module.

examples.question: An audio filter computes a 256-tap FIR filter at a sampling rate of 48 kHz. (a) How many multiply-accumulate operations per second does it need? (b) Can a 30 MHz MCU with no hardware MAC run it if each MAC costs 4 cycles? (c) What minimum DSP clock speed is needed at 1 MAC per cycle?
steps: One output sample needs one MAC per tap, so 256 MACs per sample.
The filter produces 48,000 samples per second (48 kHz = 48,000 samples/s).
Required rate = 256 × 48,000 = 12,288,000 MAC/s, that is about 12.288 M MAC/s.
On the MCU, each MAC takes 4 cycles, so the cycles needed = 12,288,000 × 4 = 49,152,000 cycles/s, which is a 49.152 MHz clock.
The MCU runs at 30 MHz = 30,000,000 cycles/s. MACs it can do = 30,000,000 ÷ 4 = 7,500,000 MAC/s = 7.5 M MAC/s.
7.5 M MAC/s is less than the 12.288 M MAC/s required, so the 30 MHz MCU cannot keep up; it supplies only 7.5 ÷ 12.288 ≈ 0.61 of the load.
A DSP does 1 MAC per cycle, so its clock must be at least 12.288 MHz. Pick 25 MHz to leave margin for loading samples, storing output and the rest of the code.
examples.answer: The filter needs 12,288,000 MAC/s (about 12.288 M MAC/s); the 30 MHz MCU manages only 7.5 M MAC/s and is too slow (it would need 49.152 MHz); a DSP clocked at 12.288 MHz or more, for example 25 MHz, can run it.

traps: Comparing a DSP and an MCU on MIPS alone. A DSP does one MAC per cycle in hardware; an MCU needs several cycles and several instructions per MAC. Convert both to MMAC/s before you compare.
Calling a microcontroller a small microprocessor. A microprocessor is a CPU with no memory; a microcontroller is a complete system with memory and peripherals on the die.

Forgetting that one MAC is two arithmetic operations (one multiply, one add). A 12.288 M MAC/s filter is doing about 24.6 million arithmetic operations per second, which is why the FLOPs figure looks twice as large.
Confusing MHz with M MAC/s. MHz is millions of cycles per second. M MAC/s = MHz ÷ cycles per MAC, so a 4-cycle MAC at 100 MHz gives 25 M MAC/s, not 100.
Quoting only the ASIC cost per chip and ignoring NRE. At low volume the NRE spread over few boards makes the ASIC far more expensive than an FPGA, even though each ASIC die costs less.

quiz.q: Name four blocks that a microcontroller has on the same die as its CPU but a microprocessor does not.
quiz.a: Flash program memory, SRAM data memory, timers, and serial ports. ADC and GPIO also count. A microprocessor needs all of these as separate external chips.

quiz.q: Which hardware unit makes a DSP fast for filters, and how many MACs per cycle does it normally give?
quiz.a: The hardware multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit, which computes a × b + c. It normally gives one MAC per cycle.

quiz.q: Why does a DSP use separate program and data buses, and what does that buy in the filter inner loop?
quiz.a: With Harvard organisation the instruction fetch and the two data operand fetches travel on different buses in the same cycle. The inner loop can therefore fetch the instruction, the coefficient h[k] and the sample x[n − k] together and feed the MAC unit every cycle. A single shared bus would need separate cycles for instruction and data, cutting throughput.

quiz.q: Why does a DSP use saturating arithmetic instead of wrapping round on overflow?
quiz.a: A wrapped result jumps from the largest positive value to the largest negative value, which in audio is a loud click and in a control loop is a violent jump. Saturation clips the result at the largest representable value, so the error stays small and bounded.

quiz.q: A 128-tap FIR filter runs at a sampling rate of 16 kHz. Find the MAC rate, and the minimum DSP clock at 1 MAC per cycle.
quiz.a: MACs per sample = 128. Samples per second = 16,000. MAC rate = 128 × 16,000 = 2,048,000 MAC/s = 2.048 M MAC/s. At 1 MAC per cycle the DSP needs at least 2.048 MHz; pick something like 10 MHz for margin.

quiz.q: A DSP at 100 MHz does 1 MAC per cycle. An MCU at 200 MHz needs 4 cycles per MAC. Which is faster for a filter, and by how much?
quiz.a: DSP: 100 MHz ÷ 1 cycle per MAC = 100 M MAC/s. MCU: 200 MHz ÷ 4 cycles per MAC = 50 M MAC/s. The DSP is twice as fast despite running at half the clock, because the MAC count, not the clock, decides filter speed.

quiz.q: A product will sell 20,000 boards. Explain why an FPGA design may be cheaper overall than an ASIC SoC, using NRE and unit cost.
quiz.a: Total cost = NRE + (unit cost × volume). An ASIC has a very large NRE (mask set) and a very small unit cost; at 20,000 boards the NRE is spread over few units, so it dominates. An FPGA has almost zero NRE and a higher unit cost, so 20,000 × higher unit cost still comes out below the ASIC total. The FPGA also reaches the market sooner, which matters if the design will change.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now blurs these four boxes: ARM Cortex-M cores ship with DSP extensions (Helium/MVE), so a single microcontroller does control and filtering. RISC-V open instruction sets let a small team build a custom SoC without a licence fee. Phone and car SoCs are built from reusable blocks called chiplets, and AI accelerators sit beside the DSP inside the same die. Search terms to follow: MAC unit, barrel shifter, saturating arithmetic, digital signal controller, NRE, FPGA versus ASIC, RISC-V SoC.
